deed: A Shalva Band of musicians with disabilities took the Eurovision stage in Tel Aviv
title: The Shalva Band of musicians with disabilities gave up "The Rising Star" because of Shabbat and went on to the Eurovision stage

trailer.text: The Shalva Band is an Israeli band of musicians with disabilities, founded in 2005 in the music therapy program of Shalva, the Israel Association for the Care and Inclusion of Persons with Disabilities.
Ahead of the Eurovision in Tel Aviv in 2019, it was considered a top contender on "The Rising Star" to represent Israel.
It withdrew from the show, because several of its members are religiously observant and taking part would have required them to desecrate Shabbat.
KAN invited it to perform as an interval act in the second semi-final.
There it performed "A Million Dreams", received a long standing ovation, and thousands of fans praised it on Twitter.

paragraphs.text: The band was founded in 2005 in the music therapy program of the Shalva organization.
It came together through its connection to the Shalva National Children's Center in Jerusalem.
Shalva provides services and programs for thousands of people with disabilities, from infancy to adulthood, and their families.
According to Kveller, the band was started by drummer Shai Ben Shushan, an IDF veteran who sustained a head injury during his service.
Shai helped found it after a long recovery from the injury.
It was founded as part of his personal rehabilitation journey.
Since then the band has performed around the country.
"The Rising Star" is an Israeli contest that determines who will represent the country at the Eurovision.
Israel has taken part in the Eurovision since 1973.
In 2019 the contest was held in Tel Aviv, after Netta Barzilai won it the previous year.
The band quickly became a favorite of the audience and viewers.
The judges praised its professionalism and its clean sound.
After its second performance it received 100% approval from the judges and the audience.
It was considered a top contender to represent Israel.
Several members of the band are religiously observant and are not willing to commit to working on Friday night or Saturday.
Eurovision contestants are required to perform in the general rehearsal, on Friday evening, 24 hours before the final.
According to one source, this rehearsal also serves the jury and acts as a backup for the live broadcast on Saturday night.
A spokesman for the European Broadcasting Union said that all broadcasters commit to the rules, including attendance at all rehearsals and live shows.
KAN and Culture Minister Miri Regev tried to convince the Union to allow the band a pre-recorded performance instead of the rehearsals.

KAN and even the Minister of Culture tried to convince the European Broadcasting Union to allow the band to skip the rehearsals in favour of a pre-recorded performance, and according to reports the union insisted that all Eurovision artists take part in all the rehearsals.
According to Israel Hayom, the band also approached the Tzomet Institute to look into Shabbat-friendly microphones and instruments.
The institute was reluctant to take on the project due to the "mass desecration of Shabbat".
The band informed Keshet that it was withdrawing, although it had already secured a place in the final.
KAN also approached singer Omer Adam with an offer to perform at the Eurovision final, but he too declined because of Shabbat.

stations.title: The invitation and the rehearsal at Expo

paragraphs.text: KAN invited the band to perform as an interval act in the second semi-final, live on May 16 in Tel Aviv.
KAN's statement said that the Eurovision slogan is "Dare to Dream", that Shalva dared to dream, and that the corporation is happy to help make dreams come true.
A week before the Eurovision, on Independence Day, the band performed at the main ceremony in Jerusalem.
Afterwards it went on the stage at Expo Tel Aviv for the first time and held a rehearsal.
That evening it held a press conference there.
Lead singer Dina Samte said that they did not get there the way they had wanted, but even so they were chosen to represent Israel, and that is a great honor.
Drummer Yosef Ovadia said that they feel the people of Israel are with them and that they are "going to blow them away".
Israel Hayom wrote that for many viewers the performance would be the highlight of the evening.
On Thursday the band went on the semi-final stage in Tel Aviv.
Millions watched the second semi-final that evening.
It went on stage just before the winners were announced, while the votes were being counted.
It performed a rendition of "A Million Dreams" from the film "The Greatest Showman".
Guitarist Sara Samuels said that the lyrics sum up the band's message well.
The band called on viewers never to stop dreaming.
At the end of the performance the audience stood up and applauded enthusiastically.
The standing ovation lasted a long time, and host Bar Refaeli appeared to be holding back tears.
Thousands of Eurovision fans praised the band on Twitter after the performance.
Viewers in Israel and abroad praised the performance.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu shared it on social media and wrote that the band had moved the world.
The official Eurovision Twitter account wrote that it is one of the most beloved acts in Israel.
According to artistic director Shai Ben Shushan, after the performance the band received numerous invitations to perform abroad.
He stressed that even on tour it would not abandon its goal of helping make life accessible to Israelis with disabilities.
According to him, the heart-warming response of the public is much more important to the band than the Eurovision.
In December 2019 the band performed "God Bless America" at the Israeli American Council summit in Hollywood, Florida, and at the end of the song its members rushed to hug President Donald Trump.
It performed with musicians from the United Arab Emirates in a virtual rendition of "Bridge Over Troubled Water", with a message of unity and peace.
According to him, today people in the street want to embrace its members, not because of a gimmick, but because they are good at what they do.
The two lead singers, Dina from India and Annael from France, are blind.
Dina Samte immigrated to Israel at the age of ten from Manipur in India.
Yosef has Williams syndrome, Yair and Tal have Down syndrome, and Guy is visually impaired.
Guitarist Sara Samuels is the daughter of the founders of the Shalva Center.
She said that people said they were crazy to do this, but they did it.
According to Kveller, the band practices four times a week.
Blogger Shlomo Brody wrote in the Times of Israel Blogs that there is irony here, because the Eurovision website presents “Inclusion, Diversity, and Unity” as a main headline.
He wrote that the offer to appear as a guest act rather than as contestants is "the epitome of being a second-class citizen".
According to him, the blame rests with Israel, which did not do enough to ensure the inclusion of religious participants in cultural and sports events.
